The Driver home was exceptionally pretty with a wealth of lavendar asters and goldenglow, the flowers being arranged throughout every room in a most artistic manner. Ferns and potted plants vied with the cut flowers in beauty and were also placed most effectively in the parlors and dining room. The affair of last evening celebrated the sixtieth anniversary of the wedding of Mr. and Mrs. Driver, who were married in London, England, August 16, 1858 and who shortly afterward came to this state to help in its upbuilding. Both Mr. and Mrs. Driver have been very active in the growth and advancement of the state and especially the city of Ogden where Mr. Driver conducted his business for many years and assisted in various ways in the upbuilding of the community. Last evening the family of Mr. and Mrs. Driver were present and assisted in receiving the guests and entertaining. The time was pleasantly spent and temptingly prepared refreshments were perfectly served during the entire evening. P Cronin, pastor of St. Patrick's church and Vicar General of the diocese, sank peacefully into the sleep that knows no earthly waking to take its flight to the bosom of her Saviour whom she loved and so faithfully served throughout her life. Suffering a fall thirteen months ago and in declining health thereafter, her death was not unexpected. Throughout her illness Mrs. Cronin never complained, but bore her sufferings with a most humble resignation to God's holy will and complete trust in the ever Sacred Heart, in which those of the true faith find comfort and support. She was born in Ireland and on May 6, 1858, was married to James Cronin in Churchtown, County Cork, coming at once to Kentucky and locating at Frankfort in 1859, but for the past forty-five years they have lived at Lexington. To their union were born nine children, of whom four are living, and whose devotion to their mother was beautiful, nursing and caring for her as any mother would her babe. She was truly a model Christian wife and mother and endeared herself to everyone. Last May Mr. and Mrs. Cronin celebrated their golden wedding, having with them their four living children, Rev. James P. and John Cronin, of Louisville, and Michael J. Cronin and Mrs. J. W. Lawrence, of Lexington. The funeral services were held Monday morning at St. Peter's church, Rev. Father Cronin being the celebrant of the solemn requiem high mass. A very touching eulogy telling of the virtues and beautiful qualities characteristic of the departed, was spoken by Rev. Father Punch, the pastor. The remains were laid to rest in the Catholic cemetery. So the pessimist who prophesied a dearth of beauty in the realm of summer dress is without honor in his own country, and no one is paying any heed to his calamatous croakings about the direful state of the autumn modes.\nFor if the poor old calamity howler made a mistake in the one instance he probably would in the other. And make a mistake he assuredly did, for never have clothes been more alluringly attractive than they are at present.\nOld Mother Nature believes in just enough variety to make us appreciate her perfections, but in midsummer she is particularly generous and gives to us of her very best. And to show that she appreciates her lavishness the August maid blossoms forth in apparel that matches the weather.\nNow is the time for the girl who is a lover of sheer raiment to indulge her fancy. What, for example, is more charming, and incidentally more \"comfy,\" for wear on warm afternoons than a pretty frock of organdie or of voile?\nDead white is trying to certain types, but a creamy tint is universally becoming.\nUnusually smart, but at the same time, delightfully simple, is the cream colored dress in which milady of the knitting needles looks so well.\nDeep bands of cream filet lace contribute that completesness of conception which always compels admiration, and the frock has attained a degree of ultra-perfection by the addition of a soft satin girdle and loop ends of old rose.\nA slipover blouse is a handy little garment to possess, and the one shown here is developed in turquoise blue in a silk and wool weave. I am feeling fine and enjoyed the overseas trip very much. I rather surprised myself. I wasn't seasick at all. At the present we are at a rest camp. We will be here for a few days, then move to our permanent camp some where further inland. Last night I took a good shower bath and cleaned up a bit, so today I am feeling fine. At the present I am, at the Y. M. C. A.\n\"This morning I went to church and enjoyed the spirit of the meeting very much. \"Now dear mother, don't you worry about me. Uncle Sam is taking good care of us. He took all precautions available to land us safely and now it is up to each one to take care of himself.\n\"We have a splendid captain and he is doing his best to make everything as comfortable as possible for us. The few old men and women I saw yesterday seemed very glad to see us. No young men to be seen; they are all at the front. I will write again when we reach our camp.\n\"Now dear mother have Bro. Carl write for you and write often, as you know letters from home are a great comfort to a soldier. I will write to the boys and sister, in a few days, as soon as I get a little better acquainted around here.\n\"Trusting this finds you all well and happy as it leaves me enjoying the best of health and of good cheer. From your loving soldier son, VICTOR. \"Address, Am. E. F., 28th Eng. C.
